opening.headline: The reason requests are being delayed while the GPU is idle is explained as a limitation of requesting GPUs by count, and DRA is examined on how it addresses this issue.
body: Even though each node has a GPU, a new pod is stuck in Pending state, and the GPU utilization shown in the dashboard is low. This is because a pod serving a small model is using only part of a GPU, yet it is occupying an entire GPU.

This lesson examines the workflow and limitations of requesting and scheduling GPUs via device plugin approach. It then explores the structure of Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA), which declares devices using classes and claims to enable filtering and sharing, the process of connecting resource claims to pods, and the roles and limitations when introducing DRA.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: This can explain the difference between device plugins and DRA.
Resource claims can be distinguished in the process of being connected to a pod.

screens.title: GPU is idle but requests are delayed
screens.lead: Check how the GPU is being utilized at each node in the diagram. By reading the utilization numbers together with the number of pending pods, you can see what's mismatched.

visual.alt: Three GPU nodes are fully occupied by a small model pod, resulting in low utilization, while a new pod remains in Pending state.
labels: One Pod occupies the entire GPU

paragraphs: There are three nodes, each with a GPU, and one pod occupies an entire GPU. Pods serving smaller models use only a portion of a GPU's resources but still exclusively occupy one full GPU.

When a new pod requests a GPU, the scheduler cannot find an available GPU. As a result, the pod is held in a Pending state. At this time, the GPU utilization displayed on the dashboard appears low, yet the request queue grows longer. This creates a contradictory situation where the device is idle while requests are being queued.

The cause lies in the approach of requesting GPUs solely by count (number). Specifying only a count cannot express requirements such as needing only a portion of a single GPU, requiring a specific capacity threshold, or allowing sharing with other pods.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: To allocate a single GPU across two workloads, what additional information should be included in the request? This lesson covers how to include that information.

screens.outro: First, let's recall how we're currently requesting a GPU.

screens.title: How are GPUs being requested and allocated?
screens.lead: When you select a question, the instructor's thought process is revealed. Since you're not submitting or entering anything, first recall your own manifest and then try it.

items.prompt: How is the GPU specified in the Pod Manifest's limits?
items.answer: Typically, we write something like `nvidia.com/gpu: 1` to indicate the type and quantity of devices. It resembles entries for CPU and memory, so it's familiar, but it's easy to miss the point that this single line requests an entire GPU.

items.prompt: How are GPU node types of different kinds distinguished?
items.answer: We cannot determine the GPU type solely based on count, so we label the nodes and send them to appropriate nodes using `nodeSelector`. The inconvenience lies in the fact that label management relies on manual human intervention.

items.prompt: Can one GPU be shared between two workloads?
items.answer: The basic request pattern does not allow expressing shared state. This limitation is why we are learning DRA today. We will examine whether there are request models that inherently support shared state and conditional specifications.

screens.outro: First, let's carefully examine the existing method of device plugins.

screens.title: GPU scheduling via device plugin method
screens.lead: In the pod manifest below, select each highlighted section and verify whether the existing approach expresses something or fails to express something.

data.text:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: embed-small
spec:
  containers:
  - name: server
    image: example.com/embedding-server:1.0
    resources:
      limits:
        nvidia.com/gpu: 1
  nodeSelector:
    example.com/gpu-model: a100

marks.note: If the administrator installs the vendor GPU driver and device plugin on a node, the cluster exposes custom scheduling resources such as `nvidia.com/gpu` or `amd.com/gpu`. This resource request specifies a full GPU. The pod may specify only limits, and if requests are also provided, they must match the limits; requests alone are not allowed. If no GPUs are available on the node, the pod remains in a Pending state.

Method for sending a pod to an appropriate node in a cluster with mixed GPU types. The label name is illustrative; if the node does not have this label, the pod will remain in Pending state. This approach circumvents the GPU type specification within the pod request by relying on node labels.

Request devices on a container basis. The device plugin approach only allows device requests per container and provides no mechanism to declare shared access to the same device across multiple containers or pods.

This approach does not support expression-based filtering. Requests that filter based on properties as conditions cannot be used if the memory capacity is above a certain threshold, and any requirements beyond count must be managed separately through label rules.

screens.outro: Let us examine the DRA model that structurally overcomes this limitation.

screens.title: Dynamic Resource Allocation: Declare a device by claiming it
screens.lead: Select each tab to review the concepts, roles, benefits, and limitations of DRA.

visual.alt: DeviceClass, ResourceSlice, ResourceClaim have a structure similar to StorageClass and PersistentVolumeClaim for storage.

tabs.label: Concept
tabs.body: Device Attachments (DRA) is a Kubernetes feature that enables pods to request and share GPU-like devices. It has been a stable feature since version 1.35 and was first introduced in version 1.30. By defining device classes accessible to device drivers and cluster administrators, workloads can claim devices from those classes. This experience is similar to how storage capacity is obtained via PersistentVolumeClaims using a StorageClass in storage.

tabs.label: Who does what one
tabs.body: There are three roles. The device owner provides a driver that supports the DRA, and the driver notifies Kubernetes of node and device information via `ResourceSlice`, and may also create `DeviceClass` if needed. The cluster administrator can attach devices to nodes, install drivers, and create `DeviceClass`. The workload operator creates either `ResourceClaim` or `ResourceClaimTemplate` and modifies the manifest to have the workload reference it.

tabs.label: advantage
tabs.body: First, device properties can be finely filtered using CEL (Common Expression Language). Second, containers or pods referencing the same claim can share a device. Third, vendor-specific device configurations can be attached to claims, enabling device configuration at the workload level rather than the node level. Fourth, device categories can be divided centrally, such as by cost-based versus high-performance classes. Fifth, workload requests need only reference claims without specifying quantities.

tabs.label: limit
tabs.body: The Kubernetes scheduler does not support preemption for DRA resources. A pod that is currently using a DRA device cannot be preempted by another pod requiring the same device with a higher priority. A high-priority pod remains in Pending state until the conflicting pod terminates or is manually deleted, freeing up the device.

screens.outro: Let's trace the order in which the claim is actually connected to the pod.

screens.title: The process of resource claims being connected to a pod
screens.lead: Let's examine the process step by step from claim creation to the device being connected to the pod. Click the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

visual.alt: The order is: claim is generated from the template, scheduler locates the device and assigns it, then the device is configured on the node.
labels: ResourceClaimTemplate → Generate a ResourceClaim for each pod (resourceclaim-controller)
Search for unassigned devices that match the conditions in ResourceSlice
Pod placement on accessible nodes of the device
References existing claims by name; deployment fails if the claim does not exist.

steps.title: Claim is prepared
steps.body: If a workload references a `ResourceClaimTemplate`, the `resourceclaim-controller` creates a `ResourceClaim` for each pod. If a specific `ResourceClaim` is directly referenced by name, the controller verifies whether the claim exists in the cluster; if it does not exist, the pod will not be deployed.

steps.title: Read the template's conditions
steps.body: The template specifies which device is desired. For example, select the category using `deviceClassName: example-device-class`, and connect the CEL filters `device.attributes["driver.example.com"].type == "gpu"` and `device.capacity["driver.example.com"].memory == quantity("64Gi")` to `&&` to ensure that only devices that are GPUs with 64Gi of memory are received. The difference between a count request and a conditional request lies in specifying attributes and capacity.

steps.title: The scheduler finds the device
steps.body: The scheduler examines ResourceSlice for each pod to find a device that satisfies two conditions: the node capable of accessing that device must be eligible to run the pod, and there must be unallocated resources matching the claim requirements.

steps.title: Allocation information is recorded
steps.body: If a suitable ResourceSlice is found, the scheduler records allocation information for the corresponding ResourceClaim. The strategy is first-fit, evaluating pools and slices in lexicographical order by name. Drivers can assign priority to slices and pools by appropriately naming them.

steps.title: The pod is deployed and the device is configured.
steps.body: After allocation is complete, the scheduler places the pod on a node that has access to the allocated device. The node's kubelet and device driver collaborate via gRPC to configure access to the device and the pod.

steps.title: Manifestation for connection reading
steps.body:
This is part of an example. The `name` of `resources.claims` must match the name of the `resourceClaims` item in the pod.

Using ``
resources:
  claims:
  - name: shared-gpu-claim
resourceClaims:
- name: shared-gpu-claim
  resourceClaimName: example-resource-claim
```

`resourceClaimTemplateName` creates a new claim for each pod, while using `resourceClaimName` uses an existing claim. If two containers reference the same `shared-gpu-claim`, they share the same GPU; containers referencing separate claims receive separate GPUs.

screens.outro: I will verify this structure with an example to illustrate how it addresses the initial issue.

screens.title: Explanation: Benefits of DRA in cases requiring GPU partitioning and sharing
screens.lead: The instructor explains an example of a small model and a large model sharing a GPU pool. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

visual.alt: Bar chart comparing GPU occupancy status before and after applying DRA.
labels: Embedding A + Embedding B (sharing the same claim)

steps.title: situation
steps.body: Two small embedding model servers and one large model server share the same GPU pool. The large model requires a GPU with ample memory, while the small model can suffice with only a portion of the GPUs.

steps.title: Step 1: Existing Method
steps.body: In the device plugin approach, all three pods request one GPU each. Since two smaller models each take a full GPU, three GPUs are required, and two of them will remain largely idle. This matches the low utilization observed in the initial scene's request.

steps.title: Step 2: Problem Analysis
steps.body: You cannot filter devices by count or type, and there is no mechanism to share a device among multiple uses. To prevent a large model from being assigned to a small GPU, you must separately manage node labels and the `nodeSelector` rules.

steps.title: Step 3: Apply DRA
steps.body: The large model creates claims with memory capacity conditions using CEL, receiving only devices that meet the requirements. Two smaller models share one device by referencing the same `ResourceClaim`. The GPU setup that previously required three GPUs is now reduced to two, and the remaining devices can be used by other workloads.

steps.title: Step 4: Class Separation
steps.body: Divide the device category into classes. Create cost-effective general-purpose classes and high-performance classes so workloads can select the one that best fits their needs. The requester does not need to know the specific model name of the device, and central management of the categories is possible.

screens.outro: We will examine the role assignments and limitations required during the introduction phase using a case study.

screens.title: Analysis: Case study on reviewing roles and limitations when introducing DRA
screens.lead: This time, the instructor will fully explain the process of introducing DRA into the existing device plugin cluster. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

steps.title: situation
steps.body: We aim to introduce DRA into a cluster that previously operated GPUs via a device plugin. The objective is to verify who is responsible for what preparation and what changes occur after the introduction.

steps.title: Step 1: Driver Verification
steps.body: To use DRA, the device must have a driver compatible with DRA. The driver creates a ResourceSlice, updates it when the device capacity changes, and configures the device according to claims, then connects it to a container. First, verify with the device vendor whether they provide a driver that supports DRA.

steps.title: Step 2: DeviceClass Design
steps.body: The cluster administrator creates a DeviceClass. By dividing classes by use case—such as a general-purpose workload class and a high-performance class for critical jobs—workload operators can make simpler selections.

steps.title: Step 3: Read the problem manifest
steps.body: The pod references `resourceClaimName: gpu-claim` but there is no ResourceClaim in the same namespace. In this case, the pod will not be created. Either create the claim first, or if each pod requires a claim, switch to using `ResourceClaimTemplate`.

steps.title: Step 4: Workload Transition
steps.body: Remove the GPU `limits` from the container and reference `resources.claims` along with the pod's `resourceClaims`. Instead of specifying quantities in the request, the claim reflects the device's condition.

steps.title: Step 5: Boundary Reflection
steps.body: DRA resources do not support preemption. Since a pod already using the resource cannot be evicted by a high-priority pod, operational guidelines should explicitly state that a high-priority pod may remain in Pending state until the resource becomes available.

screens.outro: Finally, I will summarize the content discussed so far.

screens.title: DRA declares the device as a claim
screens.lead: This lecture reviews and compares the two GPU request methods discussed.

paragraphs: The device plugin approach requests devices on a per-unit basis. It requests an entire GPU at once, allows requests per container only, and does not support sharing or expression-based filtering. GPU types are circumvented using node labels and `nodeSelector`.

DRA is a model that obtains devices as claims from a class. The driver notifies the resource slice with device information, the administrator assigns a category via DeviceClass, and the operator declares conditions using ResourceClaim or ResourceClaimTemplate. Benefits include CEL filtering, sharing via claims, workload-specific device configurations, and centralized classification through classes.
When introducing it, remember the limitation that preemptive scheduling is not supported, and that a pod will not be deployed if no ResourceClaim is referenced.

Going back to the initial scene, the GPU was idle because the request was overwhelmed, not due to insufficient hardware, but because the request could only be described as "entirely one batch." Once requests can express conditions and sharing capabilities, the same GPU pool can handle more work.

callout.label: organizing
callout.text: DRA declares the device as a claim.

glossary.def: This exposes vendor devices as scheduling resource like nvidia.com/gpu, allowing pods to request quantities via limits.
A Kubernetes feature that requests a device as a claim within a class and shares it among pods, now stable since v1.35.
This template creates a ResourceClaim for each pod referencing it.
DeviceClass is an object that defines a device category, and ResourceSlice is an object that notifies drivers of a node's device list.
This is the process of placing a pod that requested a GPU onto a node that has an appropriate device.

misconceptions.myth: DRA is merely a renamed device plugin.
misconceptions.fact: DRA provides new request models such as claim, class, CEL filtering, and device sharing. Device plugins support only per-container count requests.

misconceptions.myth: GPU just needs requests to be sent.
misconceptions.fact: In device plugin mode, the GPU must specify at least limits; if requests are specified, they must be equal to limits. Requests alone cannot be specified.

misconceptions.myth: Switching to DRA causes high-priority pods to monopolize the GPU.
misconceptions.fact: DRA resources do not support scheduler preemption. A pod with high priority may remain in Pending state until the device becomes available.

misconceptions.myth: Referencing a claim only causes the device to be automatically generated.
misconceptions.fact: If no ResourceClaim is referenced by name, the pod will not be created. Either create the claim first or use a ResourceClaimTemplate.

closing.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class.
points: DRA declares the device as a claim.
Device plugins are requested on a per-count basis and do not support sharing or filtering.
DRA classifies and requests devices using DeviceClass, ResourceSlice, ResourceClaim, and ResourceClaimTemplate.
Referencing the same claim, one device can be shared among multiple containers or pods.
